title: Aniruddha Is Brought to Usha and They Unite
story:
Chitralekha left Shonitapura the way a shadow leaves a wall — silently, in the dark, and gone. She took with her a painter's skill, the powers of a yogini trained in the secret arts, and a secret: her friend Usha, the daughter of King Bana, had dreamed of a man she had never seen. Chitralekha had painted face after face — gods, princes, the great families of men — until Usha cried out at one of them. That face belonged to Aniruddha, the grandson of Krishna, and he lived in Dvaraka, across a distance that would have taken an army a season to cross. Chitralekha crossed it in a single night.

Dvaraka lay sleeping beneath the stars. She moved through the great city like a thought, past palaces and gardens and sleeping guards, until she came to the house where Aniruddha slept. There she found him — the prince of the dream given flesh — asleep on a beautiful couch in his inner chamber, with no one to stand between him and the night. By her yogic power she gathered him up, still sleeping, and carried him back the way she had come. He did not wake. The night did not speak of it. By the time the first light came, the couch in that quiet chamber lay empty, and the dream of Shonitapura had begun to come true.

Usha was waiting. When the youth of her dream was carried into her rooms — the dark youth of the painting, real at last — her face lit with joy and all her longing fell away. She received him as a bride receives her groom. She dressed him in the finest garments, wound garlands about him, set sweet scents and incense and lamps burning about him, and placed him in the seat of honor in her chambers. And when he woke, it was not to the roof of his father's house but to the hidden heart of the guarded palace of Bana — and to the girl who had dreamed him.

So the grandson of Krishna came to live in the innermost rooms of the women's quarters of Shonitapura, and the secret held. The king's guards stood at every outer gate, and the inner chambers, where no man was ever permitted, became the safest walls in the city. Day after day passed, and no one perceived it. Usha's love deepened with every sunrise, and Aniruddha — carried sleeping into a strange kingdom — found in that hidden chamber a home and a wife. They lived as two who belong to each other, and neither of them counted the days.

But Shonitapura was Bana's city, and the walls that kept every other man out could not keep a secret in forever. Somewhere in the palace, eyes were beginning to notice the small strangenesses — an extra lamp burning late in the inner quarters, hushed voices, a princess who no longer grieved by her doorway. The days of their hidden life were passing, and each one carried the secret a day closer to the light.
reflection: The most guarded place in the asura city becomes the safest hiding place in it: the secret lives exactly where no one thinks to look, and the guards themselves become its walls. The story's quiet strangeness is that a prince is stolen by love rather than by war — carried across an impossible distance while asleep, and woken to find his life already changed.
tradition_note: The Harivamsha tells the journey differently: there, Chitralekha finds Aniruddha awake in Dvaraka, wins his heart with news of Usha, and the two are united in a secret Gandharva marriage. The Bhagavata has her carry the sleeping prince by her yogic power.
next_story_tease: But a secret kept inside Bana's own city could not stay hidden for long.
hero_scene: Under a vast night sky, Chitralekha flies above the sea of darkness between the two cities, carrying the sleeping Aniruddha in her arms, his hair and robes streaming in the wind, the towers of Dvaraka fading behind her.
